status_reasoning: Reviewers expressed significant conceptual concerns about the behavioral state definitions, noting that 'dwelling and forward locomotion as defined are mutually exclusive behaviors' and questioning whether it is 'useful to discuss them as different behavioral states that have state durations independent of one another.' They found the framework 'could be confusing' and requested 'a more intuitive description,' indicating uncertainty about whether these represent true behavioral states versus artifacts of the analysis approach.

Reviewers expressed dissatisfaction with the statistical characterization of behavioral dynamics, stating 'the conclusions regarding whether or not behavior is actively or stochastically controlled during this period are based on statistical analysis, as the data do not allow an intuitive understanding' and that 'one relies on the "black box" of statistical analysis and modeling.' They also noted confusion about terminology, stating there is 'no good a priori reason to expect the statistics to be Poissonian' and that the term 'stabilizing the forward state' is used inconsistently. The reviewers requested that authors 'explain in simple language what the data of Figure 3 means.'

While reviewers acknowledged that 'the authors show an influence of PKA signaling on the behavioral changes surrounding/during lethargus,' they expressed concern that 'PKA signaling is such a general determinant of cellular activity that it almost would have been surprising if it had no effect.' They noted that 'no detailed molecular details or neuronal control circuits can be deduced from the work,' suggesting the biological significance of the findings remains unclear despite the observed phenotypes.

Reviewers did not explicitly critique the loss-of-function phenotypes but expressed general concern that 'no detailed molecular details or neuronal control circuits can be deduced from the work' and that conclusions should be 'well-supported.' The observation that these mutants show wild-type behavior during lethargus was presented as data but its interpretation in the context of PKA's 'general' role raises questions about mechanistic understanding.

The model proposing that PKA stabilizes active wakefulness through neuropeptide release and CREB is subject to the reviewers' general concern that 'PKA signaling is such a general determinant of cellular activity' and that 'no detailed molecular details or neuronal control circuits can be deduced.' Reviewers requested that authors 'make sure conclusions drawn from the results are well-supported,' suggesting uncertainty about the mechanistic model.

Reviewers explicitly challenged the claims about regional quiescence hierarchy, stating that 'the term "hierarchy" implies that anterior segments exert control over posterior segments. This cannot be concluded from the mere observation that the anterior segments are more active.' They questioned what constitutes 'almost indistinguishable' when comparing dynamics and criticized the conclusion that 'head/neck motoneuron circuits governed the dynamics,' noting 'this conclusion again seems to rest on the assumption that if the head moves more than the rest of the body, its neural circuits must be governing the system.'

The crh-1 mutant phenotypes were not explicitly discussed by reviewers, but fall under their general concern that 'no detailed molecular details or neuronal control circuits can be deduced' and that the biological significance of PKA pathway manipulations remains unclear. The complex phenotype (poorly-defined states outside lethargus, increased directed locomotion during lethargus) would likely be subject to the reviewers' request for clearer interpretation.

Reviewers explicitly praised the technical advances, stating 'from a technical point of view there are some significant advances here: an unprecedented content-rich longitudinal study of development/behavior and novel parallel processing tools for analyzing large-scale image data.' They recommended publication 'as a methods paper plus proof-of-principle biology,' affirming the methodological contributions while requesting more detail about implementation and comparison to other systems.

The descriptive observations about gradual modulation of locomotion parameters (forward/dwelling fractions, bend velocity, bend frequency) during development were not challenged by reviewers. These represent straightforward quantitative measurements that reviewers implicitly accepted as valid data, though they questioned the interpretation of behavioral states built upon these measurements.

The claim that PKA signaling plays a minor role during lethargus is speculative and was not directly addressed by reviewers, but falls under their general concern about the lack of 'detailed molecular details or neuronal control circuits' and their request to ensure 'conclusions drawn from the results are well-supported.' The interpretation of wild-type-like behavior in loss-of-function mutants during lethargus requires mechanistic clarity that reviewers found lacking.
